case_info.scenario: An 18-year-old male with no significant medical history presented for evaluation of a nasal papule. He reported that the papule had been present for 1 year. The lesion was asymptomatic without any associated pain, pruritus, or bleeding. He did not report any trauma to the area, and it was not causing nasal obstruction. It had not grown or changed over the past year. He had never had a similar lesion. On physical examination there was a flesh-colored, well-circumscribed papule perpendicular to the nasal mucosa, protruding into the nasal cavity (Figure, A). Focused examination of the face additionally revealed a flesh-colored papule on the left tragus, clinically consistent with an accessory tragus. The nasal papule was biopsied at the base under local anesthesia with iris scissors and sent for histopathologic examination. Grossly, the lesion was a 2 × 1 × 1 mm tan papule. Microscopically the lesion was a small and well-circumscribed proliferation of spindled cells arranged as fascicles with intervening clefts (Figure, B). Some foci showed palisading of nuclei around anuclear zones (ie, Verocay bodies).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of an 18-year-old male presenting with a pedunculated papule perpendicular to the nasal mucosa. B, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained biopsy of the nasal papule (original magnification ×40).
case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

dialogue_history.text: I agree that the histopathology features are classic for schwannoma, but given the location and the associated accessory tragus, this likely represents a nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma, a benign lesion that can resemble schwannoma histologically. While schwannoma is a reasonable differential, the clinical context of a congenital nasal papule with an accessory tragus is key, and complete excision is often recommended to confirm the diagnosis and prevent local complications.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

case_info.explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9
